title: JESUS SAID SOME OF THEM WOULD NOT DIE BEFORE SEEING GOD’S KINGDOM. SO WHAT DID THEY ACTUALLY SEE?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID SOME OF THEM WOULD NOT DIE BEFORE SEEING GOD’S KINGDOM. SO WHAT DID THEY ACTUALLY SEE?

One of Jesus’ most misunderstood promises in Mark 9:1 becomes breathtakingly clear when we follow six days of silence, climb a mountain with three frightened disciples, and discover why the glory of Christ changes everything—even for people carrying a past they wish they could erase.
Imagine standing in front of Jesus.

You have abandoned things to follow Him. You have heard Him speak with an authority no religious leader ever possessed. You have watched demons surrender, sickness retreat, and desperate people find hope simply because He entered their lives.
Then, suddenly, He says something that sounds almost impossible.
“Verily I say unto you, That there be some of them that stand here, which shall not taste of death, till they have seen the kingdom of God come with power.” — Mark 9:1 (KJV)
Some of you standing here will not die until you see the Kingdom of God come with power.
Now imagine those words following you home.
You lie awake wondering what He meant.
Will Rome fall? Will heaven open? Will the Messiah finally take His throne? Will the suffering of Israel end before some of you are buried?
And here is the question that has troubled readers for centuries.
Those disciples died.
The Roman Empire continued.
The world did not end.
So was Jesus mistaken?
Did His promise fail?
Or have we been reading one of the most extraordinary declarations in the Gospel without noticing what happened immediately afterward?
Because six days later, Jesus took three men up a mountain.
And what they witnessed was so overwhelming that one of them would later write about it as an eyewitness to the majesty of Christ.
But before we climb that mountain, we need to understand something.
Jesus did not make this promise in a comfortable moment. He made it in the shadow of a cross.
And that changes everything.
Just before Mark 9:1, Jesus had begun teaching His disciples that He must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise again after three days (Mark 8:31).
Think about what that meant to people who believed the Messiah would deliver them.
They expected victory.
Jesus announced suffering.
They expected a crown.
Jesus spoke of a cross.
They expected Him to defeat their enemies.
Jesus told them that anyone who wanted to follow Him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Him.
Peter could hardly bear it.
He took Jesus aside and began rebuking Him.
Imagine that.
A disciple trying to correct the Savior.
A man who had just confessed Jesus as the Christ was now resisting the very mission for which Christ had come.
And Jesus answered with words that must have pierced Peter's heart.
“Get thee behind me, Satan: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but the things that be of men.” (Mark 8:33, KJV)
Peter wanted glory without suffering.
A kingdom without sacrifice.
A Messiah who would conquer without first being crucified.
And before we judge him, perhaps we should admit how familiar that sounds.
We want resurrection without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
A transformed life without letting Jesus confront the habits we secretly protect.
We want God to rescue us from consequences while allowing us to remain in control.
Peter's struggle was not merely an ancient misunderstanding.
It is a mirror.

Then Jesus spoke about losing one's life for His sake and the Gospel's sake. He warned against gaining the whole world and losing one's soul. He spoke of the Son of Man coming in the glory of His Father with the holy angels.
And immediately after that warning came the promise.
Some standing there would not taste death before seeing the Kingdom of God come with power.
The Greek text of Mark 9:1 contains a remarkable expression:
οὐ μὴ γεύσωνται θανάτου
ou mē geusōntai thanatou
Literally, “they shall certainly not taste death.”
The expression “taste death” is a vivid way of speaking about experiencing death. The Greek construction ou mē gives the denial particular force.
Jesus was emphatic.
He was not suggesting that those disciples would never die. He was declaring that some would witness something before their deaths.
But what?
Mark uses another striking expression:
τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει
tēn basileian tou theou elēlythuian en dynamei
The sense is “the kingdom of God having come in power.”
Notice that Jesus spoke of something they would see.
And notice what Mark tells us next.
“And after six days Jesus taketh with him Peter, and James, and John, and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves: and he was transfigured before them.” (Mark 9:2, KJV)
Six days.
Mark does not insert a long series of unrelated events between the promise and this extraordinary encounter.
He takes us straight to a mountain.
And there, three men saw something they would never forget.
Jesus was transfigured before them.
The Greek word is μετεμορφώθη (metemorphōthē), from the verb metamorphoō, meaning to be transformed or transfigured.
Mark describes His garments becoming dazzlingly white, beyond what any earthly launderer could produce.
Matthew adds that His face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2).
Luke tells us that the appearance of His face changed and His clothing became radiant (Luke 9:29).
This was not Jesus becoming divine for the first time.
He was already the eternal Son of God.
It was a moment in which His concealed glory was astonishingly disclosed to human witnesses.
The carpenter from Nazareth.
The Teacher who grew tired.
The Savior who walked dusty roads and ate with sinners.
The One who would soon be beaten, mocked, and nailed to a Roman cross.
Before their eyes, His majesty shone.
And suddenly, the promise of Mark 9:1 begins to make sense.
The cross would not be the defeat of His kingdom. The cross would be central to the victory of its King.
The disciples needed to see that the One who had predicted His suffering was not a helpless victim of history.
He was the glorious Son.
And He was going to Jerusalem willingly.
But the mountain held another surprise.
Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with Jesus.
Moses, through whom God had given the Law to Israel.
Elijah, the prophet whose ministry had powerfully confronted idolatry and called God's people back to covenant faithfulness.
Their presence was extraordinary.
Yet Luke tells us something even more extraordinary about their conversation.
They were speaking of Jesus' departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).
The Greek word translated “decease” in the King James Version is ἔξοδος (exodos).
Exodus.
Departure.
The same word that evokes the great deliverance of Israel from Egypt.

Here, in the presence of Moses, the conversation centered on the departure Jesus would accomplish in Jerusalem—His approaching death, understood in the larger context of His resurrection and saving mission.
Consider the beauty of that connection.
Through Moses, God delivered His people from bondage in Egypt.
Through Jesus Christ, God accomplishes the greater redemption that frees sinners from the condemnation and dominion of sin.
The blood of the Passover lamb pointed forward to a deeper deliverance.
And Jesus, whom John the Baptist called “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world,” was moving toward the sacrifice that would secure redemption for His people (John 1:29).
The mountain was not an escape from the cross.
It was a revelation of the glory of the One who would bear it.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because some of us have spent years asking God to reveal His glory while resisting the road of obedience.
We pray for breakthroughs.
We pray for restoration.
We pray for doors to open.
But when Jesus calls us to forgive someone, confess a hidden sin, abandon a destructive relationship, surrender our pride, or make restitution for something we have done, we suddenly become hesitant.
We want to see His power.
But we are afraid of what following Him might cost.
Peter knew that feeling.
On the mountain, overwhelmed by what he saw, he suggested making three tabernacles—one for Jesus, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.
Mark tells us plainly that Peter did not know what to say because they were terrified (Mark 9:6).
Then a cloud overshadowed them.
And a voice came from the cloud.
“This is my beloved Son: hear him.” — Mark 9:7 (KJV)
Hear Him.
Not merely admire Him.
Not simply celebrate His miracles.
Not only become emotional when His glory is revealed.
Listen to Him.
Listen when He speaks about suffering.
Listen when He commands repentance.
Listen when He teaches that following Him means taking up the cross.
Listen when He promises eternal life.
Listen when He says that the Son of Man must suffer, die, and rise again.
Moses and Elijah were extraordinary servants of God.
But Jesus is the beloved Son.
And when the disciples looked around again, they saw no one with them except Jesus.
What a picture.
The terrifying brilliance.
The ancient prophets.
The heavenly cloud.
The voice of the Father.
And when it was over—
Jesus remained.
There is a lesson here for anyone whose faith has become dependent on spiritual excitement.
Emotions rise and fall.
Circumstances change.
Powerful experiences eventually become memories.
But Christ remains.
And the deepest question is not whether you have ever experienced a moment that made you tremble.
It is whether you are listening to Jesus when the mountain is behind you and obedience becomes costly.
Now we must be careful with the interpretation.
The connection between Mark 9:1 and the Transfiguration is compelling, especially because Mark places the Transfiguration immediately afterward and explicitly mentions the six-day interval.
Matthew and Luke also place these events together.
And the apostle Peter later described the Transfiguration in language that strongly supports its significance as a revelation of Christ's royal majesty.
In 2 Peter 1:16–18, Peter insists that the apostles were not following cleverly invented stories when they proclaimed the power and coming of Jesus Christ.
They had been eyewitnesses of His majesty.
Peter recalls hearing the Father's voice on the holy mountain.
He had seen something real.
Not a religious fantasy.
Not a metaphor invented to comfort frightened believers.
He had witnessed the glory of the Son.
This is why many interpreters understand the Transfiguration as the immediate and primary fulfillment of Jesus' promise that some would see the Kingdom of God come with power.
Peter, James, and John were among those standing before Jesus when He spoke.
And before they tasted death, they witnessed a preview of the King's glory.
Yet we should not pretend that every faithful Christian interpreter agrees on every detail.

Some understand Mark 9:1 as referring primarily to Jesus' resurrection, His exaltation, the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, or the powerful advance of His kingdom through the apostolic proclamation of the Gospel.
Others connect the saying with the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70.
These interpretations arise because the Kingdom of God is revealed throughout Jesus' ministry, death, resurrection, exaltation, and the continuing work of the Gospel.
There is also an important distinction between Mark 9:1 and Mark 8:38.
Mark 8:38 explicitly speaks of the Son of Man coming in the glory of His Father with the holy angels, while Mark 9:1 speaks of seeing the Kingdom of God having come with power.
The passages are connected, but they are not worded identically.
For that reason, we should not simply assume that Mark 9:1 must describe the final return of Christ occurring within the disciples' earthly lifetimes.
The Transfiguration interpretation takes seriously both the immediate narrative and the wider biblical testimony.
It understands the mountain as a genuine foretaste of the glory that will be fully manifested when Christ returns.
The preview was not the completion.
The disciples saw His majesty.
But they had not yet witnessed the final resurrection of the dead, the last judgment, or the complete renewal of creation.
Those promises still belong to the future consummation of God's kingdom.
Jesus' resurrection and exaltation would publicly vindicate the crucified Messiah, and Pentecost would display the power of His reign through the Spirit-filled witness of His people.
The kingdom was already breaking into history through the ministry of Jesus.
Its final fulfillment was still to come.
That is not a contradiction.
It is the biblical tension between the kingdom already inaugurated and the kingdom not yet consummated.
And it matters because the same Jesus who revealed His glory on the mountain would soon be hanging on a cross.
Imagine Peter seeing that.
The face that had shone with heavenly brilliance now bruised and bleeding.
The garments that had appeared dazzlingly white now stripped away.
The beloved Son, affirmed by the Father's voice, now mocked by people who did not recognize their King.
What would Peter remember?
Would he remember the mountain?
Would he remember the voice?
Would he remember the command to listen?
We are not told everything that passed through Peter's mind at the crucifixion.
But Scripture tells us that Peter himself would fail terribly.
He would deny Jesus three times.
The man who saw the glory of Christ would later insist that he did not know Him.
Think about the tragedy of that moment.
Peter had seen what most people could only imagine.
He had witnessed the Transfiguration.
He had heard the voice from heaven.
And still, under pressure, he collapsed.
That should humble every one of us.
Spiritual experiences do not make us incapable of sin.
Biblical knowledge does not make us immune to fear.
Years of church attendance do not automatically produce a surrendered heart.
Even those who have witnessed extraordinary things must depend on the grace of God.
But Peter's story did not end in denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Lord confronted Peter with a searching question.
“Lovest thou me?”
And He entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had failed was not beyond the reach of redeeming grace.
Peter's restoration did not make his denial acceptable.
It showed that his failure was not stronger than Christ's mercy.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a private scandal for years.
Something you said.
Someone you betrayed.
A promise you broke.
A season of secret compromise.
A relationship you damaged.
A sin you keep confessing but have not yet decisively turned away from.
You still attend worship.
You still share Bible verses.
You still tell people that God is good.
But there are moments when you wonder whether Jesus could ever look at you without remembering what you did.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
He did not come to excuse evil.
He came to save sinners through His atoning death and victorious resurrection.
The call is not to hide your sin behind religious language.
It is to repent, confess, believe, and follow Him.
As 1 John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That promise is not permission to continue living in rebellion.
It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemnation their sins deserve.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for the One who redeemed us (Titus 2:11–14).
The King who shone on the mountain is the same Savior who shed His blood at Calvary.
And He is the same risen Lord who calls sinners to Himself today.
This is why Mark 9:1 is so much more than an argument about biblical chronology.
It forces us to confront the identity of Jesus.
If He is merely a religious teacher, His words about the kingdom can be treated as an interesting historical puzzle.
But if He is the beloved Son of God, revealed in glory, crucified for sinners, raised from the dead, and exalted as Lord—
Then His words demand more than curiosity.
They demand a response.
The disciples were given a glimpse of the King's glory.
We have been given the apostolic testimony that calls us to trust Him.
And we are waiting for the day when faith will become sight.
The New Testament does not promise that every believer will receive a mountaintop vision like Peter, James, and John.
It calls us to believe in Christ through the testimony God has given.
And it promises that the risen Jesus will return.
Not as a defeated Messiah.
Not as a forgotten figure of history.
But as the Lord before whom every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).
That coming day gives urgency to the present one.
Because the question is not only what the disciples saw before they died.
The question is what you will do with the Savior revealed to you in Scripture before your own earthly life comes to an end.
We spend so much of our lives postponing what matters most.
We tell ourselves we will forgive when the pain becomes smaller.
We will repent when temptation becomes weaker.
We will return to prayer when life becomes quieter.
We will seek God when our schedules become manageable.
We will surrender when we have enjoyed just a little more of the world.
But tomorrow is not guaranteed.
And the same Jesus who warned about gaining the whole world and losing one's soul still calls people to follow Him.
What if the thing you have been protecting is the very thing keeping you from walking in obedience?
What if your greatest spiritual danger is not that you have never heard the truth, but that you have become skilled at postponing your response to it?
Do not confuse being moved by a Christian article with being transformed by the Gospel.
A tear is not repentance.
A comment is not conversion.
Only Jesus saves.
And salvation is not purchased by religious activity, charitable giving, or financial support.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But genuine faith does not leave us indifferent.
It changes what we love, what we pursue, how we treat people, and how we use what God has entrusted to us.
It makes us willing to encourage others, serve the Church, share the Gospel, and support faithful ministry according to our ability and conviction.
If these words have brought something into the light, do not bury that moment beneath another distraction.
You do not need to disclose private sins publicly. God sees what others cannot, and a trusted, mature believer can help you walk toward repentance, healing, and accountability.
And think of the person who may need this truth today.
The friend who thinks one terrible mistake has disqualified them from God's mercy.
The family member who has quietly drifted from faith.
The believer who is afraid to ask difficult questions about Scripture.
The person who has been told that Christianity cannot withstand honest examination.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
But because truth worth hearing is also worth passing on.
Our desire is not simply to produce content people enjoy for a moment.
It is to point people continually toward Jesus Christ, faithful biblical understanding, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and a life of genuine discipleship.
And there is another way you can help this work continue.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel work.

Scripture encourages believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). It also recognizes the importance of supporting those who faithfully labor in teaching and proclaiming the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone who needs encouragement.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God, and the Gospel is not for sale.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that lives are brought under the transforming truth of His Word.
Because the glory revealed on that mountain was never meant to become a spectacle detached from the Savior's mission.
Jesus descended from the mountain.
He continued toward Jerusalem.
He carried the burden of the cross.
He gave His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
And on the third day, He rose.
The disciples would eventually understand that the glory they had seen was not a reason to avoid the cross.
It was a reason to trust the One who would endure it.
The King was not defeated by His suffering.
Through His death and resurrection, He accomplished the redemption He had come to secure.
And the same Peter who once tried to prevent Jesus from going to the cross would later proclaim the crucified and risen Christ with courage.
That is what grace can do.
It does not erase history.
It redeems people within history.
It does not pretend betrayal never happened.
It restores repentant sinners through the mercy of Christ.
It does not turn the cross into a minor detail.
It reveals the cross as central to God's saving purpose.
So when you read Mark 9:1 again, do not stop at the difficult question.
Follow Jesus up the mountain.
Hear the Father's voice.
Look at the beloved Son.
Then follow Him down the mountain, toward the cross, through the empty tomb, and into the hope of His promised return.
The disciples were allowed to see a preview of the glory of the King.
Today, you are invited to trust that King.
Not because every mystery has been exhausted.
Not because you have become worthy.
Not because you have finally managed to repair every broken piece of your past.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your faith.
And His grace is sufficient to receive and transform those who turn to Him.
Perhaps you came to this article wondering whether Jesus made a promise He failed to keep.
But perhaps you are leaving with a more personal question.
Have you been resisting a promise He has faithfully made?
The promise that whoever comes to Him, He will never cast out (John 6:37).
The promise of forgiveness for those who confess their sins.
The promise of eternal life to those who believe in Him.
The promise that He will come again.
You do not have to pretend you are strong.
You do not have to hide behind a religious reputation.
You do not have to manufacture a mountaintop experience.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Listen to Him.
Follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not make peace with the darkness. Return to the Savior whose mercy is greater than your failure.
Because Peter's greatest hope was never that he had once stood on a mountain and seen Jesus shine.
His greatest hope was that the glorious Jesus he had seen was also the merciful Savior who died and rose again.
And that is our hope, too.
The glory Peter saw on the mountain was breathtaking—but the grace that met him after his denial is the reason a broken sinner can still come home.
